question: Which 1995 film was the first full-length feature made entirely with computer animation?
source_excerpt: inspired leadership of the Pixar Toy Story Team resulting in the first feature-length computer animated film

extra.why_interesting: Players assume fully computer-animated features have always existed; pinning the first one to 1995 and a toy cowboy gives a satisfying anchor.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources including Oscars.org confirm Toy Story (1995) as the first feature-length computer-animated film, with Lasseter receiving a Special Achievement Oscar for it.

explanation: Pixar's debut feature took roughly four years to make and turned a cowboy doll and a space ranger into the start of a new era in animation.

question: Whitney Houston's giant 1992 ballad 'I Will Always Love You' was written and first recorded in the early 1970s by which country singer?
source_excerpt: written and originally recorded in 1973 by American singer-songwriter Dolly Parton

extra.why_interesting: Most people think of it as Whitney Houston's song; learning it was a country farewell ballad by Dolly Parton reframes it completely.
extra.verification_notes: Dolly Parton wrote and recorded 'I Will Always Love You' on June 12, 1973 (released 1974), before Whitney Houston's 1992 cover for The Bodyguard.

explanation: Parton wrote it as a farewell to her mentor Porter Wagoner, and Houston's version for The Bodyguard turned it into one of the best-selling singles ever.

question: The Lion King's carefree song 'Hakuna Matata' takes its title from a real phrase meaning 'no worries' in which African language?
source_excerpt: Hakuna matata is a Swahili phrase... it means 'there are no worries'

extra.why_interesting: Millions sing the phrase without realising it is a real expression from a real language spoken by tens of millions of people in East Africa.
extra.verification_notes: Hakuna Matata is confirmed as a Swahili phrase meaning 'no worries,' consistent with Wikipedia and all corroborating sources.

explanation: Swahili is spoken across East Africa, including Kenya and Tanzania, whose savannas inspired the film's setting.

question: In the Pixar film Finding Nemo, what kind of fish are Nemo and his father Marlin?
source_excerpt: Marlin, an overly cautious clownfish, and his son Nemo... are separated

extra.why_interesting: An instantly recognisable orange-and-white character that many players can picture but may hesitate to name as a species.
extra.verification_notes: Marlin and Nemo are clownfish (species debated as ocellaris vs. percula, but both are clownfish), per Wikipedia's plot description of Finding Nemo.

explanation: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, which is exactly where the film's family makes its home.

question: Nirvana's breakthrough hit 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' got its title from a phrase a friend scrawled on Kurt Cobain's wall. Without Cobain realising it, the phrase referred to a brand of which everyday product?
source_excerpt: Nirvana's 1991 song "Smells Like Teen Spirit" was named after this piece of graffiti by Kathleen Hanna in reference to the deodorant brand.

extra.why_interesting: The title sounds like a poetic statement about youth; discovering it references a supermarket toiletry undercuts the myth delightfully.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia and multiple sources confirm Teen Spirit was a deodorant brand (originally by Mennen) that Kathleen Hanna referenced when she wrote the graffiti on Cobain's wall, unbeknownst to him.

explanation: Kathleen Hanna wrote that Kurt smelled like Teen Spirit, the deodorant his girlfriend wore, and Cobain took it as a revolutionary slogan.

question: When MTV launched in 1981, the very first music video it broadcast had a pointedly fitting title. Which song was it?
alternative_answers: Video Killed the Radio Star by The Buggles
The Buggles - Video Killed the Radio Star
source_excerpt: The first video was "Video Killed the Radio Star" by the Buggles, played at 12:01 a.m. on August 1, 1981

extra.why_interesting: The choice was a deliberate joke about the channel's own mission, and the title can be reasoned towards once the player knows it was 'fitting'.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative sources confirm 'Video Killed the Radio Star' by The Buggles was the first video aired at MTV's launch on August 1, 1981.

explanation: The Buggles' 1979 hit was chosen as a cheeky mission statement for a channel built on music videos.

question: After starting as short sketches on another comedy show, The Simpsons first aired as its own half-hour series in which year?
source_excerpt: the series premiere of the American animated television series The Simpsons... premiered on December 17, 1989, on Fox

extra.why_interesting: The show feels timeless, so players struggle to place it; realising it predates the whole 1990s is a small shock.
extra.verification_notes: The Simpsons' first half-hour episode, 'Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire,' premiered December 17, 1989 on Fox, after starting as shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show in 1987.

explanation: The full series debuted on Fox in December 1989 with a Christmas episode, and it has run continuously ever since.

question: Which video game came first: Tetris or Super Mario Bros.?
source_excerpt: released on June 6, 1984, while he was working for the Dorodnitsyn Computing Centre of the Academy of Science of the Soviet Union

extra.why_interesting: Both are icons of 1980s gaming, and many players assume the Nintendo blockbuster came first because it defined the era.
extra.verification_notes: Tetris was released June 6, 1984, over a year before Super Mario Bros. released September 13, 1985.

explanation: Alexey Pajitnov programmed Tetris in Moscow in 1984, a year before Nintendo released Super Mario Bros. in Japan.

question: True or false: the cat Marlon Brando strokes in the opening scene of The Godfather was a stray the director found on the studio lot and placed in his lap unscripted.
source_excerpt: The cat in Marlon's hands was not planned for. I saw the cat running around the studio, and took it and put it in his hands without a word.

extra.why_interesting: The cat feels like a deliberate, symbolic directorial choice; learning it was an unplanned stray makes an iconic image feel wonderfully accidental.
extra.verification_notes: Coppola himself confirmed he found the cat running loose on the Paramount lot and put it in Brando's hands unscripted, corroborated across multiple film sources.

explanation: Coppola found the cat wandering around the Paramount lot, and its loud purring even muffled some of Brando's lines, which had to be re-recorded.

question: The mechanical shark in Steven Spielberg's Jaws was given a friendly first-name nickname on set, borrowed from Spielberg's lawyer. What was the shark called?
source_excerpt: Bruce, the Last 'Jaws' Shark, Got His Name From Spielberg's Lawyer

extra.why_interesting: A terrifying screen monster with a cosy human first name borrowed from a lawyer is a lovely contrast, and the nickname has become famous enough to be fair game.
extra.verification_notes: The mechanical shark was named 'Bruce' after Bruce Ramer, Spielberg's longtime entertainment lawyer, confirmed by Newsweek and the Jaws Wiki.

explanation: Bruce broke down so often in the salt water that Spielberg was forced to keep the shark off screen, which made the film far scarier.

question: Michael Jackson's 1983 hit 'Beat It' features a blistering guitar solo by a famous rock guitarist who was not credited on the album and reportedly did it for free. Who was he?
source_excerpt: Eddie Van Halen played an unpaid, initially uncredited solo on Michael Jackson's 'Beat It.'

extra.why_interesting: A pop king's biggest rock moment was gifted by a hard-rock guitar hero from a rival genre, and he did it for nothing.
extra.verification_notes: Eddie Van Halen recorded the uncredited, unpaid guitar solo on 'Beat It' as a favor, confirmed by multiple sources including his own recollections.

explanation: Producer Quincy Jones invited him in, and he recorded the solo in a couple of takes while his own band was out of town, asking nothing in return.

question: Paul McCartney had the tune for 'Yesterday' long before the words. Until the real lyrics came, he sang it under a placeholder title named after a breakfast dish. What was that title?
source_excerpt: 'Yesterday,' One of The Beatles' Best Songs, Was Originally Named 'Scrambled Eggs'

extra.why_interesting: The player pictures the most-covered ballad in pop history as something born fully formed and heartbroken; learning it spent months being sung about breakfast is a delightful deflation.
extra.verification_notes: Well-documented Beatles history: McCartney used placeholder lyrics 'Scrambled eggs, oh my baby how I love your legs' before finalizing 'Yesterday's real lyrics.

explanation: McCartney dreamed the melody and, fearing he'd stolen it, sang 'Scrambled eggs, oh my baby how I love your legs' for months until 'Yesterday' finally arrived.

question: The Blair Witch Project earned around 250 million dollars worldwide in 1999. Roughly how much did it cost to shoot?
source_excerpt: shot on an original budget of $35,000–$60,000, and had a final cost of $200,000–$750,000 after post-production and marketing

extra.why_interesting: Players know it was cheap, but 'cheap' for a global box-office hit usually means a few million; the real figure is the price of a family car, which makes it one of the most profitable films ever made.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources confirm the film was shot for roughly $35,000-$60,000 (tens of thousands of dollars), even though post-production/marketing pushed total costs higher.

explanation: The original shoot cost only tens of thousands of dollars, with three unknown actors, a couple of cheap cameras and a week in the Maryland woods, making it one of the most profitable films in history.

question: Two years before Marlon Brando famously refused his Best Actor Oscar for The Godfather, another actor had already turned his down, won for playing a Second World War general. Who was he?
source_excerpt: George C. Scott won Best Actor for Patton and refused the award, calling the ceremony a 'meat parade'

extra.why_interesting: Everyone remembers Brando's refusal as the first great Oscar snub; the stem gives the player the year gap and the war-general role as footholds to reach the man who actually did it first.
extra.verification_notes: George C. Scott refused Best Actor for Patton at the 43rd Academy Awards (April 15, 1971), exactly two years before Brando's refusal at the 45th Academy Awards (March 27, 1973) for The Godfather.

explanation: Scott called the Oscars a 'two-hour meat parade' and declined the award for Patton in 1971, becoming the first actor ever to refuse one.

question: Alan Rickman had never appeared in a feature film until, at 41, he played a suave villain holding a Los Angeles skyscraper hostage. Which 1988 action movie was it?
source_excerpt: Die Hard was Rickman's feature film debut at the age of 41

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a villain performance that iconic came from a seasoned screen actor, but it was Rickman's first movie role, taken in his forties after years on the stage.
extra.verification_notes: Alan Rickman, born Feb 21 1946, was 41 when Die Hard (1988) released, marking his feature film debut as Hans Gruber, villain holding Nakatomi Plaza (LA skyscraper) hostage.

explanation: Rickman was a Royal Shakespeare Company stage actor with no film credits when he was cast as Hans Gruber, and the role launched his Hollywood career overnight.

question: A hurricane that forms in the Atlantic would be called what if the very same kind of storm formed in the northwest Pacific, near Japan or the Philippines?
source_excerpt: these rotating storms are called hurricanes... in the Northwest Pacific, the same type of disturbance is called a 'typhoon'

extra.why_interesting: Players assume hurricanes and typhoons are different beasts; they are the identical storm wearing a regional name.
extra.verification_notes: NOAA confirms tropical cyclones are called hurricanes in the Atlantic and typhoons in the Northwest Pacific near Japan/Philippines, a stable naming convention.

explanation: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are all the same rotating tropical storm, and the label depends purely on which ocean basin it spins up in.

question: The shoreline of which body of water, shared by Israel and Jordan, is the lowest point on dry land anywhere on Earth?
source_excerpt: the lowest elevation and the lowest body of water on the surface of Earth

extra.why_interesting: Players think of the lowest place on Earth as somewhere in the ocean; the lowest walkable ground is a beach you can actually stand on.
extra.verification_notes: The Dead Sea, bordered by Israel and Jordan, is universally cited as the lowest point on dry land on Earth, currently around 430-440m below sea level.

explanation: Its shore lies more than 430 metres below sea level, and the water level keeps dropping by about a metre a year, so the record only gets deeper.

question: Which gas makes up almost four fifths of the air you are breathing right now?
source_excerpt: Nitrogen (N2), 78.08%, Oxygen (O2), 20.95%

extra.why_interesting: People instinctively say oxygen because it is the gas we care about; the gas we mostly inhale does nothing for us at all.
extra.verification_notes: Nitrogen makes up approximately 78% of Earth's atmosphere by volume, which is 'almost four fifths' as claimed.

explanation: Air is about 78 percent nitrogen and only 21 percent oxygen, so most of every breath goes in and straight back out unused.

question: The centre of the Earth is hotter than the surface of the sun. Is the innermost core solid, liquid, or gas?
source_excerpt: Earth's inner core is the innermost geologic layer of the planet Earth. It is primarily a solid ball with a radius of about 1,220 km

extra.why_interesting: Everyone pictures the centre of the Earth as a molten sea; the very middle is actually a solid ball hotter than the sun's surface.
extra.verification_notes: Earth's inner core is confirmed to be a solid iron-nickel sphere kept solid by extreme pressure despite temperatures hotter than the sun's surface; 2026 'superionic state' research refines the atomic-scale picture but the iron lattice itself remains solid.

explanation: The pressure at the centre is so enormous that iron and nickel stay locked in a solid ball, while the layer around it, the outer core, is the one that is molten.

question: Earth's continents drift across the planet at roughly the same speed as which part of the human body grows?
source_excerpt: the crust moved at 20 millimeters per year, which is nearly the speed at which fingernails grow

extra.why_interesting: Continents feel eternally fixed, yet they crawl at a speed the player can literally measure on their own hand.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple authoritative science sources confirm continental drift rates (~1-10 cm/year) are commonly compared to fingernail growth rate, a well-established trivia fact.

explanation: Tectonic plates move a few centimetres a year, about the pace of a growing fingernail, which is enough to have opened the whole Atlantic Ocean over tens of millions of years.

question: Which single lake, in Siberia, holds roughly one fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the Earth's surface?
source_excerpt: Lake Baikal is the deepest and most voluminous freshwater lake in the world... containing some 20% of the world's total unfrozen freshwater reserve

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the Great Lakes or the Amazon to hold the big fresh water number; a single Siberian lake beats them all.
extra.verification_notes: UNESCO and Britannica confirm Lake Baikal holds approximately 20% (one-fifth) of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater, a stable geological fact.

explanation: At over 1,600 metres, it is the deepest lake on Earth, so it stores more fresh water than all five North American Great Lakes combined.

question: The word 'tsunami' is Japanese and combines two words. One means 'wave'. What does the other mean?
source_excerpt: A tsunami is a Japanese word meaning 'harbour wave'... 'tsu' (harbour) and 'nami' (wave)

extra.why_interesting: The word is used worldwide, yet almost nobody knows it describes not the open sea but the place where the wave does its damage.
extra.verification_notes: Tsunami is composed of Japanese 'tsu' (harbour) and 'nami' (wave), per Wikipedia and Etymonline.

explanation: Fishermen out at sea would notice nothing unusual, then return to find their harbour destroyed, so the word literally means 'harbour wave'.

question: Across the whole planet, roughly how many lightning strikes hit the ground or sea in a single day?
source_excerpt: the global per-second flash rate ranges from 35 flashes per second during the Northern hemisphere winter to 55 flashes per second during the Northern hemisphere summer

extra.why_interesting: A single storm feels like a big event; the player has to accept that the planet is being hit millions of times before they finish dinner.
extra.verification_notes: NASA Earthdata and NOAA sources put daily global cloud-to-ground lightning strikes in the low-to-high millions (roughly 1-8 million/day depending on methodology), confirming 'Millions' as the correct order of magnitude.

explanation: Earth takes around 100 strikes every second, which adds up to roughly 8 million a day, mostly over tropical land like the Congo Basin.

question: Measured from its base on the sea floor to its summit, which Hawaiian volcano is taller than Mount Everest?
source_excerpt: Mauna Kea rises more than 10,200 meters (33,500 feet) from its base on the Pacific seafloor to its summit

extra.why_interesting: Everest is only the champion if you start counting at sea level; the real giant is mostly hidden under the Pacific, and the player must pick the right Hawaiian peak.
extra.verification_notes: Mauna Kea rises ~10,200 m (33,500 ft) from its base on the Pacific seafloor to its summit, taller than Everest's ~8,849 m above sea level, making it the tallest mountain base-to-summit.

explanation: Only about 4,200 metres of it stand above the sea, but the volcano rises more than 10,000 metres from the ocean floor, over a kilometre more than Everest.

question: Every year, millions of tonnes of dust cross the Atlantic and deliver phosphorus that fertilises the Amazon rainforest. Which desert does that dust come from?
source_excerpt: 27.7 million tons of dust... makes the journey, riding the trade winds across roughly 1,600 miles of ocean before falling over the Amazon

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the Amazon as self-sufficient and a desert as lifeless; the overturn is that the wettest forest on Earth is fed by dust from the driest place, blown across an entire ocean.
extra.verification_notes: NASA satellite (CALIPSO) research confirms ~27 million tonnes of Saharan dust, including phosphorus mainly from Chad's Bodélé Depression, cross the Atlantic yearly to fertilize Amazon soils.

explanation: Rain constantly washes nutrients out of Amazon soil, and Saharan dust blown across the ocean tops up the phosphorus the forest would otherwise lose.

question: Point Nemo in the South Pacific is the spot in the ocean farthest from any land, about 2,700 kilometres in every direction. When a ship passes through, the nearest other humans are often not on land or sea at all. Where are they?
source_excerpt: the closest human beings are astronauts on the International Space Station, should the ISS be passing overhead at the time

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the nearest people to a remote ocean spot are on some island or ship; the overturn is that land is so far away that people orbiting above the atmosphere are often nearer.
extra.verification_notes: ISS orbits at ~400km altitude, far closer to Point Nemo than the ~2,688km nearest landmass, and remains crewed/operational through at least 2030 per current NASA/ESA plans.

explanation: The station orbits only about 400 kilometres up, so when it passes overhead its crew are far closer to Point Nemo than anyone on shore.

question: The toy brand name LEGO is squeezed together from two Danish words meaning what?
source_excerpt: The name 'LEGO' is an abbreviation of the two Danish words "leg godt", meaning "play well".

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a brand name is just a made-up sound; it turns out to be a tiny instruction in Danish.
extra.verification_notes: LEGO's official company history confirms the name derives from Danish 'leg godt' meaning 'play well'.

explanation: Founder Ole Kirk Christiansen took it from the Danish phrase 'leg godt', which simply means 'play well'.

question: The colourful twisting cube puzzle that became a worldwide craze in the 1980s was invented by a professor of architecture from which country?
source_excerpt: invented in 1974 by Hungarian sculptor and professor of architecture Ernő Rubik

extra.why_interesting: The puzzle feels global and nationless, yet it came out of a Budapest classroom behind the Iron Curtain.
extra.verification_notes: Ernő Rubik, a Hungarian professor of architecture at the Budapest College of Applied Arts, invented the cube in 1974 and it became a global craze in the 1980s.

explanation: Ernő Rubik built the first cube in Budapest in 1974, originally calling it the Magic Cube.

question: The word 'robot' was coined for a 1920 stage play and comes from a word meaning forced labour in which language?
source_excerpt: from the Czech word robota, which means "forced labor"

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a science-fiction word to be English or Greek; it was coined for a stage play in Prague.
extra.verification_notes: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. coined 'robot' from the Czech word 'robota' meaning forced labour/drudgery, per NPR and MIT Press sources.

explanation: Karel Čapek used it in his play R.U.R., and credited his brother Josef with suggesting the word.

question: The wireless technology that pairs your phone with your car is named after a tenth-century king of which country?
source_excerpt: King Harald Bluetooth... was famous for uniting Scandinavia just as we intended to unite the PC and cellular industries

extra.why_interesting: A name that sounds like marketing nonsense is actually a thousand-year-old Viking king's nickname.
extra.verification_notes: Bluetooth is officially named after Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson, 10th-century king of Denmark, per Bluetooth SIG's own account.

explanation: Harald Bluetooth united Danish tribes, so engineers borrowed his name for a standard meant to unite devices, and the logo merges his runic initials.

question: The word 'quarantine' comes from the Venetian word for a specific number of days that ships had to wait offshore during plague times. How many days?
source_excerpt: from quaranta giorni, literally 'forty days'

extra.why_interesting: A word everyone used daily in 2020 has a precise number hidden inside it that almost nobody noticed.
extra.verification_notes: Etymonline and multiple sources confirm 'quarantine' derives from Venetian/Italian 'quaranta giorni' (forty days), the isolation period for ships during plague times.

explanation: Venetian 'quarantena' means forty days, the isolation period imposed on arriving ships in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

question: QR codes were invented in Japan in 1994 to track components on the production line of which industry?
source_excerpt: the QR Code was invented by DENSO WAVE in 1994 to help manage the production of car parts

extra.why_interesting: A code now on every restaurant menu was built for a factory floor, not for phones, which did not even have cameras yet.
extra.verification_notes: Denso Wave invented the QR code in 1994 specifically for tracking automotive parts on the production line; confirmed by Denso's own official history page.

explanation: Denso Wave, a Toyota subsidiary, needed a code that could hold more data than a barcode and be scanned quickly on the assembly line.

question: True or false: the word 'emoji' is derived from the word 'emotion'.
source_excerpt: comes from Japanese e "picture" + moji "character"; the resemblance to emotion and emoticon is coincidental.

extra.why_interesting: The player is almost certain the word is built from 'emotion', and the truth is a pure coincidence across two languages.
extra.verification_notes: "Emoji" derives from Japanese e (picture) + moji (character), coined ~1999 by Shigetaka Kurita; resemblance to "emotion" is coincidental, per Etymonline.

explanation: Emoji is Japanese for 'picture character', from 'e' meaning picture and 'moji' meaning character, and its similarity to 'emotion' is pure coincidence.

question: Three of these food words reached us from the Aztec language Nahuatl. Which one did not?
source_excerpt: The word avocado comes from the Nahuatl ahuacatl... tomato takes its name from the Nahuatl tomatl... chocolate comes from the Nahuatl xocolātl

extra.why_interesting: All four are New World foods with Spanish-sounding names, so the player has to know which language the Spanish borrowed each from.
extra.verification_notes: Chocolate, tomato, and avocado derive from Nahuatl (xocolātl, tomatl, ahuacatl), while potato comes from Spanish patata via Taino batata, per Merriam-Webster's Nahuatl word series.

explanation: Chocolate, tomato and avocado all come from Nahuatl words, but potato comes from the Caribbean Taíno word 'batata', borrowed through Spanish.

question: The word for a horse-drawn carriage known as a coach, which later gave its name to long-distance buses, comes from the name of a village in which country?
source_excerpt: Kocs is a village...famous for having given its name to the carriage known as a coach

extra.why_interesting: A word used across half of Europe for carriages and buses traces back to one small village most players have never heard of.
extra.verification_notes: The word 'coach' derives from Kocs, a Hungarian village famed for carriage-making in the 15th-16th centuries; the term later extended to long-distance buses in British English.

explanation: Carriages built in the village of Kocs in the fifteenth century were so admired that 'kocsi' spread into German, English, Slovak, Czech and many other languages.

question: On a standard six-sided die, which number is always on the face directly opposite the six?
source_excerpt: the opposite faces of standard dice always sum to seven: six is opposite one, five is opposite two, and three is opposite four

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has held a die a thousand times, yet most players have never consciously noticed the opposite faces obey a rule; once said aloud, it feels obvious.
extra.verification_notes: Standard Western dice follow the convention that opposite faces sum to seven, so the face opposite six is one.

explanation: Opposite faces of a standard die always add up to seven, so the six sits back-to-back with the one, the five with the two, and the four with the three.

question: The word 'denim' is a shortening of a French phrase that names the city where the cloth was associated. Which city?
source_excerpt: The term denim dates back to the 17th century and originates from the city of Nîmes, in the south of France.

extra.why_interesting: Denim feels quintessentially American, so players reach for the Wild West; the word actually hides the name of a Roman-era city in the south of France.
extra.verification_notes: Denim derives from 'serge de Nîmes,' referring to Nîmes, France, a well-documented etymology.

explanation: The sturdy fabric was known as 'serge de Nîmes', and the last two words simply fused into 'denim', while the word 'jeans' points to another cloth-trading city, Genoa.

question: The world's most famous restaurant star ratings are awarded by a guide that was launched in 1900 to sell which product?
source_excerpt: The Michelin Guides ... are a series of guide books ... published by the French tyre company Michelin since 1900.

extra.why_interesting: Players think of stars for restaurants as coming from a food critic institution; the twist is that the guide exists to sell tyres by getting people to drive further.
extra.verification_notes: Michelin Guide was launched in 1900 by the French tyre company Michelin to promote automobile travel and boost tyre sales.

explanation: The Michelin brothers gave the guide away free to French motorists, hoping that more driving would wear out more tyres.

question: After falling out with his brother Adi in the 1940s, Rudolf Dassler founded which sportswear brand, still based in the same small German town as Adidas?
source_excerpt: In January 1948, Rudi registered his company as Schuhfabrik Rudolf Dassler, or "RUDA," and within the year, he changed the business name to PUMA

extra.why_interesting: Two of the fiercest rivals in sportswear were born from one family quarrel in one small town, and both still sit on opposite sides of the same river.
extra.verification_notes: Rudolf Dassler split from brother Adi in 1948, founded RUDA which became Puma later that year; both Puma and Adidas remain headquartered in Herzogenaurach, Germany.

explanation: The feud split the town of Herzogenaurach so deeply that locals reportedly checked which shoes a stranger was wearing before speaking to them.

question: In May 2010, a programmer in Florida made the first recorded real-world purchase with bitcoin, paying ten thousand coins for what?
source_excerpt: Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas delivered from Papa John's, an act considered to be the first real-world bitcoin transaction

extra.why_interesting: A sum that later became worth hundreds of millions of dollars bought something you could eat in one evening.
extra.verification_notes: Laszlo Hanyecz, a Jacksonville, Florida programmer, paid 10,000 BTC on May 22, 2010 for two Papa John's pizzas, the first recorded real-world bitcoin transaction.

explanation: Bitcoin fans still mark 22 May as Bitcoin Pizza Day, since those ten thousand coins would later be worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

question: Long before mobile phones, the Finnish company Nokia was founded in 1865 as a mill producing which material?
source_excerpt: In 1865, the mining engineer, Fredrik Idestam established a ground wood pulp mill on the banks of the Tammerkoski rapids in the town of Tampere

extra.why_interesting: The company that once dominated the mobile phone market started in the most analogue business imaginable, grinding wood into pulp.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Fredrik Idestam established a ground wood pulp mill in Tampere in 1865, which became Nokia.

explanation: Nokia spent its first century making pulp, rubber boots and cables before it ever touched a phone.

question: Since 2008, the British car brands Jaguar and Land Rover have been owned by a conglomerate headquartered in which country?
source_excerpt: Jaguar Land Rover is a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Motors Limited, part of the Tata group

extra.why_interesting: Two of Britain's most quintessentially British car brands have been owned for years by a company from a former British colony.
extra.verification_notes: JLR has been a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Motors (Tata Group), headquartered in Mumbai, India, since the 2008 acquisition from Ford; this remains true in 2026 despite an internal Tata Motors demerger.

explanation: Tata Motors bought both brands from Ford, and Jaguar Land Rover has since become the group's biggest earner.

question: During a hyperinflation crisis in 2009, which African country issued a banknote with a face value of one hundred trillion dollars?
source_excerpt: The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe introduced the $100 trillion banknote on 16 January 2009

extra.why_interesting: A single banknote carried a number most people have never seen written on anything, and it could barely buy a bus ticket.
extra.verification_notes: Zimbabwe's Reserve Bank issued the $100 trillion note on 16 January 2009 during hyperinflation, confirmed by Wikipedia.

explanation: The note was worth only a few US dollars when printed, and the country abandoned its own currency shortly afterwards.

question: True or false: the Swiss watchmaker Rolex is owned by a charitable foundation rather than by shareholders or a family.
source_excerpt: The Hans Wilsdorf Foundation... is the sole owner of Rolex SA

extra.why_interesting: The ultimate symbol of private wealth is not owned by a billionaire family or listed on any stock exchange, but by a charity.
extra.verification_notes: Rolex S.A. is 100% owned by the Hans Wilsdorf Foundation, a private charitable trust under Swiss law since 1960, confirming the claimed 'True' answer.

explanation: Founder Hans Wilsdorf left the company to a foundation in his name, which is why Rolex publishes no accounts and is famously secretive.

question: The world's oldest central bank, founded in 1668, today funds the Nobel memorial prize in economics. Which country does it belong to?
source_excerpt: The Bank of the Estates of the Realm – today Sveriges Riksbank – was established in 1668 and is the world's oldest central bank.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Britain or Italy as the home of banking; the answer is a country better known for furniture and pop music, and the Nobel clue gives a fair path to it.
extra.verification_notes: Sveriges Riksbank, founded 1668, is confirmed as the world's oldest surviving central bank and funds the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

explanation: The Riksbank predates the Bank of England by 26 years, and it created the economics prize in 1968 to mark its 300th birthday.

question: Which French car manufacturer has been making pepper mills since the 1870s and still sells them to restaurants today?
source_excerpt: The story of Peugeot's mills began in 1874 with the Z model... it was then made in silver-plated metal, in bakelite, in wood

extra.why_interesting: Players know Peugeot only as a carmaker; discovering the same lion-badged company has been grinding pepper on restaurant tables for 150 years, and still does, is a genuine double-take.
extra.verification_notes: Peugeot's first purpose-built pepper mill (the Z model) launched in 1874, and Peugeot Saveurs continues to manufacture and sell pepper mills today.

explanation: The Peugeot family began with steel tools and coffee mills in the 1840s, added pepper mills in 1874, and only built its first car years after that.
